newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany bids to calm forex mkts, but fails.
newsitem.headline: Germany bids to calm forex mkts, but fails.

text.p: Germany tried on Wednesday to calm foreign exchange turbulence that has hammered the mark in recent weeks, but markets were unconvinced by what they saw as a weak verbal defence of Europe's anchor currency.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, addressing a banking conference in Stuttgart in the evening, reinforced a message delivered earlier in a government statement as he played down the recent weakening of the mark.
"Short term currency fluctuations are no grounds for worry," he said.

Waigel said there were always "fluctuations and speculative exaggerations" between major currencies and said the current strength of the dollar and the pound sterling reflected economic conditions in the U.S. and Britain.
The comments had minimal market impact, with the dollar still trading at a robust 1.7944 marks at 1700 GMT.

Analysts had already dismissed as inadequate a similar statement by government spokesman Peter Hausmann, following a cabinet meeting at which Chancellor Helmut Kohl and his ministers discussed the mark's recent slide.
"From a German perspective there is no reason to dramatise recent developments on foreign exchange markets," Hausmann told a regular government news conference in Bonn.
The mark has been steadily losing ground against the dollar and the pound as markets become increasingly convinced Europe's planned single currency will be weaker than the mark when launched in 1999.
Waigel said markets had no justification for doubting the stability of the euro.
"Nothing is being softened or interpreted in a lax manner here," he said.

The very idea of currency devaluation is anathema to Germans who often recall the two periods of hyperinflation they have suffered in this century as they insist that Europe's currency must be as strong as the mark has been.

As the dollar touched 1.80 marks last week, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer weighed in, saying the long-awaited correction in the mark exchange rates was now well overdone and the mark had to enter monetary union as a strong currency.
Waigel on Tuesday tried to rein in markets by hinting at coordinated central bank intervention by Germany and its international partners.

But markets have shrugged off these efforts and after a confusing series of mixed signals from the government, independent analysts said this latest effort to calm the unruly waters of foreign exchange markets was bound to backfire.

"The expectation had been that they would use much stronger wording than they did. We expect the markets to react to this in the opposite way -- that is by selling the mark and buying the dollar," said Gerd Mueller of BHF Bank.
And that is exactly what happened.
Instead of throwing a lifeline to the sinking mark, the government's efforts appeared to push it deeper into the waters of speculation and uncertainty about European monetary union.
The dollar at one point hit a European session high of 1.8010 marks on Wednesday, close to the 71-month peak of 1.8040 it scaled on Tuesday.
Nick Parsons, forex strategist at Banque Paribas in London, said the market was not comforted by Bonn's words.

"It's an invitation to sell more marks," he said. "This is not just a phenomenon which is driven by dollar strength, this is a period of all-round mark weakness and reflects insecurity about the German economy and EMU."
Dealers also said there was a real risk of central bank intervention and that the government was sending clear signals about this to the market.
